study_type: Preclinical animal and human cohort study
key_claims: Endothelial cells release soluble, full-length Delta-like ligand 4 (Dll4), which increases with age and drives both primary and secondary sarcopenia.
Dll4 accumulates in interstitial spaces by binding to type I collagen and selectively activates Notch2, causing impaired muscle function, endothelial senescence, and vascular regression.
Sustained inhibition of Dll4 attenuates primary sarcopenia, preserves vascular integrity, improves systemic aging phenotypes, and extends lifespan in mouse models, even when started in aged mice.
Human cohort and mouse model data show a kidney-vascular-muscle axis where renal dysfunction leads to elevated circulating Dll4, and blocking Dll4 prevents secondary sarcopenia.
limitations: Therapeutic interventions, lifespan extension, and functional outcomes were primarily demonstrated in mouse models.
The source does not outline specific human therapeutic clinical trials or establish safety profiles for Dll4 inhibition in humans.
what_not_to_say: Do not claim that Dll4-inhibiting drugs are currently approved or proven safe and effective for treating sarcopenia or extending lifespan in humans.
Do not infer tissue-specific botanical, anti-inflammatory, joint, enzymatic, or mucosal benefits, as surrogate clock scores or markers do not measure these direct tissue outcomes.
Do not give medical advice or claim that kidney disease directly causes muscle loss in humans without acknowledging the preclinical nature of the mechanistic intervention.
